lines.text: Today you will type your first real Python code and make the computer talk back to you.
Python is a real programming language that professional coders use every day.
Scientists, game makers and website builders all use it.
You type words, and the computer follows them.
The print() command shows a message on the screen.
Put your message inside the brackets, like print("Hello").
Each print starts a new line.
Text in quotes is called a string.
You can use "double" or 'single' quotes, but both ends must match.
Forget a quote and Python shows an error.
A line that starts with # is a comment.
Python skips it completely.
Use comments to explain your code or to switch a line off.
Three quotes in a row make a string that can cover many lines.
That is perfect for drawing pictures and posters with keyboard symbols.
Watch me type the word print, then round brackets, then a message in quotes.
When I press Run, Python shows exactly what was inside the quotes.
Three print lines give us three lines of output, in the same order.
Python always runs your code from top to bottom, one line at a time.
Lines that start with a hash sign are comments, so Python skips them.
Football never shows up, because we turned that line into a comment.
Three quote marks let one string stretch across many lines.
Every space you type stays exactly where you put it, so you can draw pictures.
Here the closing quote is missing, so Python does not know where the text ends.
An error is not a disaster, it is a clue. Read it, fix it, and run again.
Great work! Let’s remember what we learned.
Now build along, then try the challenges. You’ve got this!
